questions.q: Motivation is best defined as the processes accounting for an individual’s …
options: Intensity, direction and persistence of effort
questions.why: Motivation is intensity (how hard), direction (toward what) and persistence (for how long).

questions.q: In the motivation definition, ‘direction’ refers to …
questions.why: Direction is where effort points; high intensity aimed wrongly wastes everything.

questions.q: Which discipline pairing are the parents of Micro OB?
questions.why: Micro OB (individual + group, incl. motivation) draws on psychology and social psychology.

questions.q: Macro OB (organisation theory) is chiefly concerned with …
questions.why: Macro OB studies the whole organisation in its context; its parents are sociology, economics, political science.

questions.q: In Maslow’s hierarchy, which need is satisfied internally rather than externally?
questions.why: Lower needs are satisfied externally (pay, security); higher needs (esteem, self-actualisation) internally.

questions.q: The correct ascending order of Maslow’s needs is …
questions.why: Physiological → safety → social-belongingness → esteem → self-actualisation.

questions.q: Prof. Jha’s ‘fast-forward advantage’ describes Maslow as …
options: Famous and quick to explain but thin on evidence
questions.why: Maslow is intuitively loved but poorly supported; needs don’t queue in a neat order.

questions.q: In Herzberg’s theory, pay and working conditions are …
questions.why: Pay, policy, supervision and conditions are extrinsic hygiene factors; they only prevent dissatisfaction.

questions.q: According to Herzberg, the opposite of ‘dissatisfaction’ is …
questions.why: Satisfaction and dissatisfaction run on separate scales; removing a hygiene problem yields only ‘no dissatisfaction.’

questions.q: Which is a Herzberg motivator (intrinsic)?
questions.why: Motivators are about the work itself: achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement, growth.

questions.q: A common methodological criticism of Herzberg’s study is that people …
options: Credit themselves for good times and blame surroundings for bad ones
questions.why: Self-serving attribution biases the two lists, a classic critique of the method.

questions.q: High need-for-achievement individuals prefer goals with …
questions.why: They want to stretch, not gamble; easy wins give no satisfaction, impossible ones no challenge.

questions.q: McClelland found the best managers tend to be …
questions.why: Effective managers tend to be high on need for power and lower on need for affiliation.

questions.q: Alderfer’s ERG collapses Maslow’s five needs into …
questions.why: ERG = Existence (physio+safety), Relatedness (social), Growth (esteem+self-actualisation).

questions.q: ERG’s ‘frustration-regression’ principle says …
options: Blocked lower needs raise higher ones
Needs must be satisfied in order
A blocked higher need increases demand for a lower one
questions.why: Block relatedness and the person compensates by demanding more existence (e.g. higher pay).

questions.q: Offshore rigs pay a premium mainly because …
options: Frustrated relatedness regresses to existence demands
questions.why: Isolation frustrates relatedness, which regresses to ‘at least pay me more’ — the ERG mechanism.

questions.q: Self-Determination Theory’s three psychological needs are …
questions.why: SDT: autonomy (control), competence (mastery) and relatedness (connection).

questions.q: Cognitive evaluation theory predicts that paying someone for a task they already enjoy will …
questions.why: Extrinsic reward can crowd out intrinsic motivation — the Marcia/animal-shelter example.

questions.q: Locke’s goal-setting theory says the most effective goals are …
questions.why: Specific + difficult (once accepted) + feedback drives the highest performance.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three factors shaping whether goals work?
questions.why: The three are goal commitment, task characteristics and national culture.

questions.q: MBO operationalises goal-setting by …
options: Cascading specific, verifiable, time-bound goals through every level
Letting employees set any goal they like
questions.why: Management by Objectives cascades org-wide goals down, set participatively.

questions.q: The Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal illustrates that goals …
options: Have a dark side when unrealistic and tied to rewards
questions.why: Aggressive goals tied to rewards invited cheating — ‘dose carefully.’

questions.q: The single strongest source of self-efficacy (Bandura) is …
questions.why: Actually doing the task successfully builds belief most powerfully.

questions.q: Vicarious modelling works best when the model is …
questions.why: Watching a peer with a similar handicap helps; watching Tiger Woods does not.

questions.q: The Pygmalion effect is a …
options: Self-fulfilling prophecy where expectation creates the result
questions.why: Believing in someone (e.g. a hard goal) raises their self-efficacy and real performance.

questions.q: Reinforcement theory differs from goal-setting because it …
options: Ignores inner state and looks only at consequences
questions.why: Reinforcement is behaviourist; behaviour is a function of its consequences.

questions.q: Social-learning theory adds to operant conditioning the idea that we also learn by …
questions.why: We learn vicariously by observing models, not only by direct experience.

questions.q: The four processes in social-learning theory are attention, retention, motor reproduction and …
questions.why: Attention → retention → motor reproduction → reinforcement decide a model’s influence.

questions.q: In expectancy theory, ‘instrumentality’ is the link between …
questions.why: Instrumentality = Performance → Reward: ‘if I perform, will I be rewarded?’

questions.q: ‘Valence’ in expectancy theory asks …
options: Can I perform if I try?
Is the reward something I actually want?
questions.why: Valence is the value of the reward to the person; a promotion is worthless to one who wanted cash.

questions.q: Why does a zero on any one expectancy link collapse motivation?
options: Because the three are multiplied together
questions.why: Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence; a zero anywhere zeroes the product.

questions.q: Cafeteria-style rewards are designed to fix a problem of …
questions.why: Letting people choose their reward raises valence — the photo-with-CEO example.

questions.q: Equity theory says satisfaction depends on …
options: The ratio of one’s outcomes to inputs versus a referent
questions.why: We compare our outcome/input ratio to a referent; mismatch produces felt inequity.

questions.q: Biprajeet (₹40k) is less satisfied than Aneesha (₹20k) because …
options: His referent is higher-paid managers elsewhere
questions.why: Changing the referent changed the felt ratio — higher pay, lower satisfaction.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the six responses to felt inequity?
questions.why: The six are: change inputs, change outcomes, distort self, distort others, change referent, or leave.

questions.q: ‘Were we given truthful explanations for the decision?’ is which kind of justice?
questions.why: Informational justice concerns honest explanations; interpersonal concerns dignity and respect.

questions.q: Treating people with dignity and respect is which justice type?
questions.why: Interpersonal justice is about respectful treatment of individuals.

questions.q: Job engagement is best described as …
options: Investing physical, cognitive and emotional energy in the work
questions.why: Engagement is deeper than satisfaction — full investment of self in the work.

questions.q: A noted ‘dark side’ of very high engagement is …
questions.why: Over-engagement can spill into burnout — ‘too much of a good thing.’

questions.q: The integrated model of motivation is built on the spine of which theory?
questions.why: Effort → Performance → Rewards → Personal goals is the expectancy spine, with other theories slotted in.

questions.q: In the JCM, which three dimensions build ‘experienced meaningfulness’?
options: Skill variety, task identity, task significance
questions.why: Variety + identity + significance build meaningfulness; autonomy builds responsibility; feedback builds knowledge of results.

questions.q: In the MPS formula, which two dimensions are multipliers (so zero in either zeroes the score)?
questions.why: MPS = [(SV+TI+TS)/3] × Autonomy × Feedback; autonomy and feedback multiply.

questions.q: Task significance is highest for which job?
questions.why: Task significance is how much the work affects others’ lives; an ICU nurse scores high.

questions.q: Job enrichment (vs rotation) means …
options: Adding higher-level responsibility and meaning (vertical depth)
questions.why: Enrichment adds depth and purpose, rooted in Herzberg’s motivators; rotation adds variety horizontally.

questions.q: The fundraiser-meets-scholarship-student study showed relational job design can …
questions.why: Seeing the beneficiary raised persistence by 42% and nearly doubled funds raised.

questions.q: Telecommuting’s ‘out of sight, out of mind’ risk mainly costs remote workers …
questions.why: Invisibility can quietly cost remote workers advancement despite good performance.

questions.q: Works councils and board representatives are forms of …
questions.why: Representative participation; its motivational effect is weaker than direct participation.

questions.q: ‘We talk, but they don’t listen’ warns that EIP …
options: Is worse than not asking if input is ignored
questions.why: Soliciting input then ignoring it damages procedural justice more than not asking.

questions.q: Pay structure balances internal equity (job evaluation) against …
questions.why: Internal equity = worth to the org; external equity = market competitiveness via surveys.

questions.q: Which variable-pay type is most tempted toward ‘quantity over quality’?
questions.why: Piece-rate pays per unit, which can sacrifice quality for volume.

questions.q: ESOPs lift performance only when employees …
options: Psychologically feel ownership and have a real say
questions.why: Stock ownership motivates only with genuine felt ownership and voice.

questions.q: Flexible (cafeteria) benefits are the concrete expression of which expectancy concept?
questions.why: Different people value different benefits — tailoring raises valence.

questions.q: The great advantage of recognition programmes is that praise is …
questions.why: Recognition costs little but strongly affects self-esteem and self-efficacy.

questions.q: Costco paying above its rivals and getting higher productivity illustrates …
options: A leading pay strategy that pays for itself
questions.why: Leading the market can yield higher productivity and lower turnover.

questions.q: Gainsharing’s biggest design risk is …
questions.why: The fairness of how gains are split is everything; it can also raise stress.

questions.q: In the Shivani case, the drivers’ dominant motivation level is …
questions.why: Cash to feed the family dominates; relatedness and esteem go largely unmet.

questions.q: The Shivani incentive scheme combined goal-setting with which other theory?
questions.why: A specific accepted target plus a reward tied to hitting it is expectancy in action.

questions.q: Capping the Shivani incentive after drivers raised output is a textbook case of …
questions.why: Clawing back a promised reward breaks the Performance→Reward link and feels unjust.

questions.q: A high-nAch person in the integrated model is notable because they …
options: Jump straight from effort to personal goals, internally driven
questions.why: High achievers are internally driven and bypass the organisation’s extrinsic rewards.

questions.q: Self-concordance refers to …
options: How well goal reasons fit one’s own values
questions.why: Goals pursued for intrinsic, value-aligned reasons make people happier and fit better.

questions.q: Prof. Jha’s Mowgli example (child raised by animals) illustrates the … view.
questions.why: Mowgli shows you are a product of your surroundings — the nurture side.

questions.q: Phrenology (reading head-shape to predict criminality) was used to illustrate the … view.
questions.why: It stands for ‘you are born who you are’ — the discredited nature extreme.

questions.q: Herzberg’s theory, despite method criticism, is noted as widely used in …
options: Asian settings including Japan and India
questions.why: It remains hugely influential, including across Asia.

questions.q: Frank quitting a $24/hr Jeep line for a $15/hr print shop (‘brain turning to JELL-O’) motivates which tool?
questions.why: Monotony on the line is exactly what rotation/enrichment exist to fix.

questions.q: In Shivani Carriers, FTL (Full Truck Load) differs from PTL/LTL in that FTL means …
options: One client’s goods fill one truck to one destination
questions.why: FTL = one client, one truck, one destination; PTL/LTL shares a trailer and handles goods repeatedly.

questions.q: A group, in OB terms, is two or more people who …
options: Interact, are interdependent, and pursue a shared objective
questions.why: The defining trio is interaction, interdependence and a shared objective.

questions.q: An informal group is often more influential than a formal one because it …
options: Runs on trust and genuine interest, not authority
questions.why: Informal groups draw power from trust rather than organisational mandate.

questions.q: Feeling proud when your team wins a contract you weren’t part of is …
questions.why: You internalise the group, so its success becomes your success.

questions.q: Ingroup favouritism is dangerous for a manager because it …
options: Develops unconsciously even with good intentions
questions.why: Spending more informal time with one sub-team breeds favouritism without anyone intending it.

questions.q: Nick’s “not competent” remark is an example of …
questions.why: Challenging a group’s competence damages self-esteem and harms later performance.

questions.q: The punctuated-equilibrium model applies to …
options: Temporary groups with a fixed deadline
questions.why: It describes deadline-driven temporary groups, not permanent ones.

questions.q: In punctuated equilibrium, major change happens at …
questions.why: The midpoint transition is the crisis of awareness that triggers recalibration.

questions.q: Your own understanding of how you should behave in a role is …
questions.why: Role perception is self-understanding; role expectations are how others think you should behave.

questions.q: The unwritten agreement of mutual obligations between employee and organisation is the …
questions.why: Violating the psychological contract sharply reduces motivation and performance.

questions.q: The UAE team needing slow relationship-building while Sun demanded speed illustrates …
questions.why: Two legitimate but incompatible role demands at once is role conflict.

questions.q: The Stanford Prison Experiment’s main lesson is that people …
options: Don’t just perform roles — they become them
questions.why: Random role assignment produced such immersion the study was stopped after six days.

questions.q: Norms form through all of these EXCEPT …
questions.why: Norms form via early behaviours, critical events, leader statements and primacy.

questions.q: Asch’s line experiments demonstrated …
options: Conformity to obviously wrong group answers
questions.why: About 75% eventually matched a clearly wrong group answer at least once.

questions.q: The Hawthorne effect showed productivity rose because workers …
options: Knew they were observed and felt special
questions.why: Social recognition and group membership mattered more than physical conditions.

questions.q: Gossip can be functional when it …
questions.why: Protective gossip about cheaters can actually increase cooperation.

questions.q: Sabotage and theft fall under which category of deviant workplace behaviour?
questions.why: Property deviance = sabotage and stealing; political = rumours/favouritism.

questions.q: Status, per status characteristics theory, derives from all EXCEPT …
questions.why: The three sources are power, contribution ability and group-valued personal characteristics.

questions.q: High-status group members tend to …
options: Speak more and deviate from norms more freely
questions.why: Status buys airtime and latitude to bend norms; low-status members conform more.

questions.q: Social loafing increases when …
questions.why: Lost accountability is the driver; the effect grows with group size.

questions.q: Compared with the West, social loafing in collectivist cultures (China, Japan, India) is …
questions.why: Collectivist members feel more responsible to the group, reducing loafing.

questions.q: The most dangerous cohesiveness quadrant is …
questions.why: A tight team that coheres around disengagement or deviance is the worst outcome.

questions.q: Which is NOT a way to build cohesiveness?
options: Reward individuals rather than the group
questions.why: Group rewards (not individual) build cohesion; the rest are valid methods.

questions.q: Differences in values and work norms that emerge over time are …
questions.why: Deep-level diversity drives real conflict and reveals itself through interaction.

questions.q: A faultline is best described as …
options: An invisible crack-line where aligned attributes split a group
questions.why: Like a geological fault, it’s where the group breaks when pressure comes.

questions.q: Groupthink is …
questions.why: The drive for unanimity suppresses dissent and critical evaluation.

questions.q: Groups amplifying members’ pre-existing leanings is …
questions.why: Cautious groups get more cautious, risky groups riskier — discussion produces extremity.

questions.q: Which decision technique produces the highest-quality ideas?
questions.why: NGT’s silent idea-writing removes social pressure, yielding most and best ideas.

questions.q: A way to PREVENT groupthink is to …
options: Let the leader state their view first
questions.why: A formal devil’s advocate, small size and leader-withholding-opinion all reduce groupthink.

questions.q: The key difference between a work group and a work team is …
options: Synergy: a team produces output exceeding the sum of inputs
questions.why: Teams generate positive synergy and mutual accountability; groups don’t.

questions.q: Roughly what share of employees actually prefer working in teams?
questions.why: Only ~25% prefer teamwork even though ~95% say teams matter.

questions.q: Problem-solving teams’ key limitation is that they …
options: Recommend but rarely have authority to implement
questions.why: Their value is diagnosis and suggestion, not execution.

questions.q: Self-managed teams critically depend on …
questions.why: Members must feel safe to speak up and create productive conflict.

questions.q: The four conditions for effective virtual teams include all EXCEPT …
questions.why: The fourth condition is that the team is NOT made invisible to decision-makers.

questions.q: Greg James’s 45-person team was effectively a …
questions.why: Four interdependent sub-teams with a shared goal — managed wrongly as one big group.

questions.q: Across the team-effectiveness model, trust is …
options: The single most important climate variable
questions.why: Trust lets members coordinate without monitoring; it’s fragile and must be maintained.

questions.q: Which Big Five trait matters most for team performance?
questions.why: Conscientious members back up teammates and follow through.

questions.q: With 40 high- and 40 low-conscientiousness people, research suggests …
questions.why: Pure clusters yield higher overall performance than even mixing.

questions.q: James’s team notably lacked which two of the nine team roles?
questions.why: No linker (coordinator) and no controller (quality/rules enforcer).

questions.q: Bezos’s “two-pizza rule” supports an optimal team size of about …
questions.why: Research confirms 5–9 members is optimal; above 10 loafing and complexity rise.

questions.q: A team’s capacity to self-correct its plan is called …
questions.why: Reflexivity is adapting the plan when conditions demand.

questions.q: Knowing who on the team is best at what, and routing tasks accordingly, is …
questions.why: Transactive memory is part of a shared mental model.

questions.q: Which conflict type can IMPROVE outcomes when moderate?
questions.why: Moderate task conflict forces critical evaluation; relationship conflict almost always harms.

questions.q: Across 52 studies, one of the strongest predictors of team performance is …
questions.why: Trust outweighed even prior performance history as a predictor.

questions.q: To turn individuals into team players, the SELECT lever means …
questions.why: The best individual performer is often not the best team member.

questions.q: Hallmark and Whole Foods illustrate which lever?
questions.why: They added group/team-weighted rewards to signal valued behaviour.

questions.q: A team is appropriate only if the work passes which three tests?
questions.why: Use a team when the work is complex, genuinely collective, and interdependent.

questions.q: Swimming relay scoring (each races alone, scores added) illustrates …
options: Low interdependency — a team may not be needed
questions.why: Pooled, additive output signals low interdependency, unlike soccer.

questions.q: The central lesson of the Greg James case is that he …
options: Applied co-located habits to a distributed team
questions.why: Distributed teams require deliberately designed coordination he never built.

questions.q: Every failure in the HS Holdings crisis traces most directly to …
questions.why: People held different beliefs about who owned which responsibility.

questions.q: “Out of sight, out of mind” making non-US teams invisible reflects a failure of which virtual-team condition?
questions.why: Publicising efforts and staying visible to decision-makers is a core virtual-team condition.

questions.q: A firm announcing ‘we’re reorganising into teams’ without changing coordination, rewards or accountability has …
questions.why: Without earned synergy and mutual accountability, it’s a relabel, not a team.

questions.q: Starbucks’ Via instant-coffee launch (production + PR + comms + marketing) is an example of a … team.
questions.why: Same-level members from different departments on one task is cross-functional.

questions.q: The Mann Gulch fire (1949) is used to show that …
options: Crises test teams hardest when structure breaks under pressure
questions.why: It illustrates structural breakdown under extreme pressure.

questions.q: Social categorisation means we tend to see …
options: The outgroup as all alike while keeping the ingroup as individuals
questions.why: ‘They’ become one flat category; ‘we’ keep our distinct personalities.

questions.q: The India team lumping Americans and British together as one ‘Anglo’ category shows …
questions.why: Outgroup members lose internal distinction, even across different nationalities.

questions.q: The term ‘groupthink’ came from analysis of …
options: US foreign-policy fiascos such as the Bay of Pigs invasion
questions.why: Irving Janis coined the term in 1972, studying decisions like the Bay of Pigs invasion, where advisers stayed silent rather than seem disloyal.

questions.q: Groupthink is best summarised as …
options: Cohesiveness (staying as one) overriding effectiveness (deciding well)
questions.why: Harmony pressure beats realistic appraisal; 12 Angry Men is the antidote.

questions.q: Disagreement about the work itself, which can be healthy, is …
questions.why: Task conflict surfaces more ways to see a problem; the danger is it turning emotional.

questions.q: When task conflict curdles into ‘this person is out to get me,’ it has become …
questions.why: Emotional/relationship conflict is almost always destructive, as with Nick–Praveen.

questions.q: Face-to-face is called ‘rich media’ because …
options: It carries more cues (expression, gesture, tone), so conflict resolves OR escalates fast
questions.why: Lean virtual media makes misunderstanding likelier and conflict fester longer.

questions.q: ‘Follow the sun’ 24/7 support exists primarily because …
options: It is a premium product clients pay extra for
questions.why: Always-on support is a sellable moat; a 9-to-5 competitor loses the deal.

questions.q: Offshoring (vs onshoring) means support delivered …
options: From a cheaper distant location, e.g. India for a US client
questions.why: Offshore = cheaper but distant; onshore = costlier but local, faster, same culture.

questions.q: US staff doing client-facing work while India did back-end work was driven mainly by …
options: Client trust and cultural familiarity (accent, small talk)
questions.why: Clients warm to shared accent and references, creating the status split that bred resentment.

questions.q: Hofstede’s work showed that …
options: National cultures differ on measurable dimensions (e.g. power distance)
questions.why: His IBM-subsidiary study mapped dimensions like power distance and individualism-collectivism.

questions.q: ‘Power distance’ refers to a culture’s …
questions.why: High power distance = deference to hierarchy; the Colonel said it ‘always works’ in his field.

questions.q: In the SPLIT diagnostic for distributed teams, the letters stand for …
questions.why: SPLIT buckets every fix: Structure, Process, Language, Identity, Technology.

questions.q: Rotating who gets the inconvenient meeting slot is an application of …
questions.why: ‘If I’m inconvenienced, others should be too’ — shared fairness over one team always suffering.

questions.q: The professor’s leadership test contrasted ‘keeping tabs’ with …
options: Opening doors (‘what can I do so you perform better?’)
questions.why: James only monitored; a leader removes barriers and enables performance.

questions.q: When the right answer is clear but the organisation resists, the framework offered was …
questions.why: Exit (leave), Voice (stay and push for change), or Loyalty (stay and accept).

questions.q: Most people, faced with a frustrating organisation, default to …
questions.why: Voice feels risky and exit drastic, so silent loyalty is the common default, though voice is often the responsible path.

questions.q: Organisational structure defines how job tasks are …
questions.why: Those three verbs — divide, group, coordinate — are the core definition.

questions.q: How narrow each person’s job is reflects which element?
questions.why: Specialisation is the degree to which activities are divided into distinct jobs.

questions.q: Grouping all engineers together and all accountants together is …
questions.why: Functional groups similar specialists; Acme and Jones’s kitchen use it.

questions.q: Unity of command means each employee …
questions.why: One boss prevents conflicting instructions and paralysis.

questions.q: A wide span of control produces an organisation that is …
questions.why: Wide spans mean fewer managers and flatter hierarchies — cheaper and faster, if work is routine.

questions.q: Concentrating decision-making at the top is …
questions.why: Centralisation = decisions at the top; Acme is the case example.

questions.q: The degree to which jobs are governed by written rules and procedures is …
questions.why: Formalisation is standardisation through rules, descriptions and policies.

questions.q: Ford’s moving assembly line cutting Model T chassis assembly from about 12.5 hours to about 1.5 hours illustrates …
questions.why: Narrow specialised tasks raised productivity sharply — the rising part of the curve.

questions.q: ‘Human diseconomies’ of specialisation include all EXCEPT …
questions.why: Faster mastery is a gain; the diseconomies are boredom, absenteeism, errors, turnover.

questions.q: For complex, knowledge-based work, the optimal specialisation point moves …
questions.why: Complex/creative work turns negative sooner, so the optimum is lower (left).

questions.q: Kitchen → runner → pantry → floor is which departmentalisation?
questions.why: Grouping around workflow stages is process departmentalisation.

questions.q: HDFC’s retail/corporate/private-wealth split is which departmentalisation?
questions.why: Grouping by type of customer served is customer departmentalisation.

questions.q: With 4,096 workers, widening the span from 4 to 8 mainly …
questions.why: Span 8 needs 585 managers over 4 levels vs 1,365 over 6 with span 4: flatter and cheaper.

questions.q: Amul’s structure is best described as …
questions.why: Farmers and local cooperatives decide locally; the federation handles processing/distribution.

questions.q: ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3 mission control exemplifies …
questions.why: Every command rehearsed and documented — you can’t ‘wing it’ landing on the Moon.

questions.q: Communicating across formal group boundaries is …
questions.why: Boundary spanning raises knowledge transfer and innovation; Omega’s engineer does it by design.

questions.q: A Simple Structure’s biggest weakness is …
questions.why: Flat and centralised is fast but fragile and unscalable.

questions.q: Indian Railways and a passport office best illustrate a …
questions.why: Highly standardised, rule-bound, high-volume routine work is bureaucracy.

questions.q: The functional structure’s classic weakness is …
questions.why: Deep silos and a ‘not my job’ culture across functions.

questions.q: A divisional structure’s typical downside is …
options: Slow decisions only at the top
questions.why: Each division duplicates resources and may compete with the others.

questions.q: Which structure violates unity of command by design?
questions.why: Matrix gives employees two bosses (functional + project) simultaneously.

questions.q: Zomato/Swiggy core tech and early Airbnb illustrate a …
questions.why: A small core outsourcing major functions to external partners is a virtual structure.

questions.q: The matrix’s most dangerous feature is …
options: The dual reporting line creating role conflict
questions.why: Two legitimate authorities pulling on one person is organisational-level role conflict.

questions.q: In a mechanistic model, information flow is …
questions.why: Mechanistic = top-down filtered flow; organic = anyone-to-anyone.

questions.q: Organic structures are best suited to …
options: Dynamic environments, innovation and novel problems
questions.why: Fluidity and decentralisation fit change and innovation.

questions.q: Acme is the case example of a … structure; Omega of a … one.
questions.why: Acme = mechanistic (rules, hierarchy); Omega = organic (fluid, collective).

questions.q: The four contingency factors are strategy, size, technology and …
questions.why: Strategy, organisation size, technology and environment determine the right design.

questions.q: An innovation strategy calls for which structure?
questions.why: Innovation needs flexibility and experimentation — organic.

questions.q: A cost-minimisation strategy calls for which structure?
questions.why: Efficiency and volume favour tight, standardised mechanistic design.

questions.q: An imitation strategy is best served by …
questions.why: Mechanistic for proven products, selective organic for adaptation.

questions.q: Larger organisation size pushes structure toward …
questions.why: Coordinating many people requires rules and hierarchy small firms don’t need.

questions.q: Routine technology pushes toward …
questions.why: Same inputs → same outputs (assembly line) suits mechanistic design.

questions.q: A stable environment pushes toward …
questions.why: Predictable conditions allow long planning horizons and tight structure.

questions.q: Downsizing is best defined as …
options: A systematic, permanent workforce reduction as redesign
questions.why: It is an architectural decision, not a short-term cost measure.

questions.q: ‘Survivor syndrome’ appears when firms …
options: Cut payroll without redesigning the work
questions.why: Remaining staff carry more burden, morale drops, knowledge leaves.

questions.q: High formalisation tends to …
options: Reduce errors in routine work but cut initiative in novel ones
questions.why: Rules cut routine errors but suppress going-beyond-the-role.

questions.q: Decentralisation is associated with higher satisfaction and commitment, but only when employees …
options: Feel genuinely capable of the responsibility
questions.why: Autonomy motivates only if people feel able to handle it.

questions.q: High need-for-clarity individuals perform best in …
questions.why: They prefer defined roles and rules; high need-for-autonomy people prefer organic.

questions.q: In The Restaurant, Stage 1 (three people do everything) is a …
questions.why: Flat, centralised, low-formalisation — like a kirana store.

questions.q: Jones’s span of control was first exceeded around …
questions.why: Growth meant he could no longer supervise everyone, forcing the first management layer.

questions.q: At Stage 3 Jones’s hardest new requirement was supervisors with …
questions.why: Technical skill is testable; the ability to motivate and manage conflict is much harder to assess.

questions.q: Jones’s central Stage 4 dilemma is …
questions.why: Gaining the benefits of formalisation without losing the warmth that built loyalty.

questions.q: The recommended Operations Manager role mainly provides …
questions.why: It owns the kitchen-to-customer handoff and resolves cross-departmental disputes.

questions.q: A new problem the recommended restaurant structure can create is …
questions.why: Rules can become ends in themselves and departments can blame each other.

questions.q: Acme and Omega differ most fundamentally in their …
questions.why: Same parent/product/market/city — opposite structures, by deliberate choice.

questions.q: Rawls bans written memos at Omega because he believes …
options: Org charts and memos build artificial barriers between specialists
questions.why: He wants people to walk over and talk, dissolving departmental boundaries.

questions.q: Acme’s ‘one-man band’ problem is a downside of …
questions.why: Concentrated decisions create a bottleneck and starve managers of information.

questions.q: The honest verdict on ‘which structure is better, Acme or Omega?’ is …
questions.why: Mechanistic wins in stable settings; organic wins when the environment changes.

questions.q: Omega’s most valuable organisational asset is …
questions.why: Breadth and distributed knowledge make it more adaptable, if less profitable now.

questions.q: ‘Structure is strategy made visible’ means …
options: Reporting lines and rules are leadership choices shaping what the org can do
questions.why: Design decisions determine capability, speed and who wants to work there.

questions.q: The Udupi-franchise analogy (every outlet identical, idli always the same) describes …
questions.why: Fixed, documented, identical process is mechanistic — Acme.

questions.q: The ‘Zerodha/Razorpay in their first fifty people’ analogy describes …
questions.why: Blurred roles, everyone talking to everyone, fast rearrangement is organic — Omega.

questions.q: In the professor’s three-dimension map, ‘complexity’ is made up of horizontal differentiation, spatial differentiation and …
questions.why: Complexity = horizontal (division of labour) + vertical (layers) + spatial (locations).

questions.q: ‘Horizontal differentiation’ is the professor’s term for …
options: Division of labour / specialisation across jobs
questions.why: Horizontal = specialisation across jobs; vertical = layers; spatial = geography.

questions.q: The Strategic Constituencies model says an organisation structures itself around …
options: Whoever is most critical to its survival
questions.why: Regulated US airlines elevated lawyers because winning routes was the survival issue.

questions.q: US airlines once being run by lawyers illustrates that …
options: The survival-critical function rises to the top (strategic constituencies)
questions.why: When route rights decided success, legal expertise became the constituency that ran the firm.

questions.q: A key point about effectiveness measures is that they …
options: Often pull in different directions across stakeholders
Are the same for all firms
Always move in the same direction
questions.why: Employee, customer, shareholder and compliance goals frequently conflict.

questions.q: The learning curve behind specialisation shows that performance gains …
questions.why: Early effort yields fast gains, then performance flattens, the basis for specialisation’s ceiling.

questions.q: Job enlargement differs from job enrichment/enhancement in that enlargement …
options: Adds more tasks of the same level (which may not motivate)
Gives part of the boss’s job
questions.why: Enlargement = more same-level tasks; enrichment/enhancement adds higher-level responsibility.

questions.q: The Parliament Street post office single-window experiment showed that reducing strict specialisation …
options: Raised both throughput and employee satisfaction
questions.why: Single-window cut queues and raised satisfaction, task variety helped employees too.

questions.q: The professor argued the dying justification for supervision is …
questions.why: Control (keeping tabs) is increasingly hard to justify; coordination still adds value.

questions.q: ‘In-process quality control’ means …
options: Each next step checks the previous step’s quality
A separate inspector at the end of the line
questions.why: It replaces end-of-line inspection, so fewer dedicated controllers are needed.

questions.q: The KFC vs ‘Kasma Fried Chicken’ example makes the point that …
options: Hierarchy costs money, so each layer must add value
questions.why: Extra managerial layers raise overheads, letting a leaner rival undercut on price.

questions.q: A narrow span of control produces a … hierarchy; a wide span a … one.
questions.why: Fewer reports per manager means more layers (tall); more reports means fewer layers (flat).

questions.q: In the fly-in-the-soup example, ‘controlling the premises of the decision’ means …
options: Letting waiters comp up to 5 soups freely, then reviewing
questions.why: It is decentralised and bounded at once, autonomy within a tracked limit.

questions.q: Karl Weick’s idea of ‘enactment’ holds that …
options: The environment is objective and fixed
There is no single objective environment; we see what we’re trained and motivated to see
questions.why: Training and self-interest shape perception, so firms read the same facts differently.

questions.q: Boundary spanning is primarily about the boundary between …
questions.why: Boundary spanners (HR, sales, top management) read and interpret the outside world.

questions.q: The three routes to standardisation the professor gave are formalisation, professional socialisation and …
questions.why: Socialisation (e.g. MindTree, Four Seasons, Udupi) builds consistency through culture, not rules.

questions.q: Structural inertia explains why …
options: Rules accumulate over time because adding is easier than deleting
questions.why: Stability brings resistance; old rules linger as new ones are added, breeding bureaucracy.

questions.q: Theory Y (McGregor) assumes that …
options: People will work if the work is fulfilling
People dislike work and must be controlled
questions.why: Theory Y underpins self-managed teams; poor effort signals bad job design, not laziness.

questions.q: Toyota’s Jidoka (andon cord) illustrates …
options: Authority pushed to the front line (any operator can stop the line)
questions.why: Trusting the operator to halt production shows decentralised authority and quality ownership.

questions.q: Theory Z / the Japanese value order cited (country>company>family>individual) helped explain …
options: Low supervision costs and high performance
questions.why: People worked without being watched, cutting the need for supervision.

questions.q: ‘Weaponised incompetence’ means …
options: Pretending you can’t do a task so you’re never asked to
questions.why: It is turf protection; the professor stressed most skills can in fact be learned.

questions.q: Differentiation must be balanced by integration, where integration includes …
questions.why: Integration (teams, all-hands, shared goals) pulls specialised units back together.

questions.q: ‘Casualisation’ and the resulting ‘precarity’ refer to …
options: The shift to switch-on/switch-off gig labour and the insecurity it creates
questions.why: Casualisation drives the gig economy; precarity is its social cost (e.g. delayed families).

questions.q: ‘Exploitation’ (vs exploration) means an organisation is good at …
options: Doing known work cheaper, better, faster
questions.why: Exploitation = refining the known (Acme); exploration = inventing the new (Omega).

questions.q: In the photocopier contract, Omega delivered on time with zero defects mainly because …
options: Department heads decided together and everyone owned the whole product
questions.why: Organic collaboration caught the cable error and solved the missing-part problem fast.

questions.q: Acme shipped late with defects largely because …
options: Everything routed through Tyler and people stayed in their silos
questions.why: Centralised, siloed working created bottlenecks and turf wars under time pressure.

questions.q: ‘Ambidexterity’ in organisation design means being able to …
options: Do both exploitation and exploration at once
questions.why: Modern firms must exploit the known and explore the new simultaneously.

questions.q: Toyota’s reduction of setup/changeover time helped create …
questions.why: Cutting changeover time broke the old customised-costly vs standardised-cheap trade-off.

questions.q: ‘It’s lonely at the top’ (the John Tyler / Roman Catholic Church point) means …
options: Centralisation makes the org expect the boss to know everything, which no one can
questions.why: God-like omniscience is projected onto the hierarchical superior, an impossible expectation.

questions.q: The investor-vs-employee paradox (Friedman’s Walmart test, CMC Limited) shows that …
options: We prefer to WORK at Omega but INVEST in Acme, so the world drifts toward Acme
questions.why: When the two expectations conflict, the investor usually wins, eroding work-life balance.

questions.q: Most mergers (e.g. a hypothetical Acme + Omega) fail because of …
options: Cultural mismatch between the two organisations
questions.why: Complementary skills on paper are undone by clashing cultures; shareholder value often falls.

questions.q: Why does ambidexterity stay hard in practice?
options: Best people, career paths and rewards all gravitate to exploitation (the known, revenue-earning work)
questions.why: The future (exploration) is starved because incentives and talent flow to the present.

questions.q: ‘Delegation’ differs from ‘relegation’ in that delegation …
options: Prepares people, gives resources, praises and corrects
questions.why: Relegation is offloading the monkey; delegation is genuine empowerment with support.

questions.q: The kirana owner keeping his notebook despite a better billing app shows that change management is really about …
options: Managing the loss of the old (habit, mastery, identity)
Proving the new tool is better
questions.why: People mourn the old thing; the resistance isn’t about the tool’s merits.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the six forces for change?
questions.why: The six are workforce, technology, economic shocks, competition, social trends, world politics.

questions.q: Demonetisation hitting cash businesses overnight is an example of which force?
questions.why: An unpredicted event that instantly forces new ways of working is an economic shock.

questions.q: Planned change is best defined as change that is …
questions.why: Planned change is deliberate, aiming to improve adaptability and alter behaviour.

questions.q: An organisation has truly changed only when …
questions.why: Behaviour change, not documents, is the real test of change.

questions.q: Boards often hire outsiders as change agents because outsiders …
questions.why: An outsider has no investment in the status quo — Jess Westerly fits this exactly.

questions.q: A little resistance to change is actually healthy because it …
options: Brings stability and surfaces genuine flaws
questions.why: Functional conflict can improve the plan; the danger is resistance going underground.

questions.q: The most dangerous form of resistance is …
questions.why: Quiet, deferred resistance is invisible until adoption collapses months later.

questions.q: A townhall where everyone nods and no one objects is best read as …
questions.why: Silence can be the resistance; treat it as data, not consent.

questions.q: ‘I prefer a familiar problem to an unfamiliar promise’ captures which source of resistance?
questions.why: Fear of the unknown keeps people in situations they dislike.

questions.q: Reading the slide that says your region is safe and skipping the one that says the model is dying is …
questions.why: We filter information to protect the world we’ve already built.

questions.q: ‘The same audit trails that create stability defend the old way like antibodies’ describes …
questions.why: Structural inertia: built-in mechanisms producing sameness resist change.

questions.q: Changing one subsystem while the rest pulls it back is …
questions.why: Interconnected subsystems (the baby’s mobile) snap a half-change back.

questions.q: Your strongest specialists sometimes resist hardest because of …
questions.why: A change that elevates a new skill devalues masters of the old one.

questions.q: The deepest engine of resistance in the Jess Westerly case is …
questions.why: Call patterns were the consultants’ decision; taking it threatened their power.

questions.q: Among the eight tactics, communication mainly cures resistance caused by …
questions.why: If people understand and still lose something, more talking won’t help.

questions.q: Why does participation reduce resistance?
options: It’s hard to fight a decision you helped make
questions.why: Co-creation turns fingerprints into commitment — but you must mean it.

questions.q: Trust as a buffer for change is described as …
options: A bank account that must be full before the announcement
questions.why: A change is a big withdrawal; the account is filled in normal times.

questions.q: Which tactic clearly ‘crosses the ethical line’?
questions.why: Covert influence and fake roles detonate when discovered, destroying credibility.

questions.q: Honest cooptation (vs manipulation) means giving a critic …
options: A real design role with power to change the plan
questions.why: The difference is whether you’re genuinely willing to be changed by them.

questions.q: Coercion is characterised as …
options: Fastest, but highest later resentment and underground disengagement
questions.why: Direct threats get surface compliance fast and quiet disengagement later.

questions.q: Lewin’s three steps, in order, are …
questions.why: Melt the status quo, move to the new state, then refreeze so it sticks.

questions.q: In force-field analysis, the smarter and cheaper move is usually to …
questions.why: Reducing restraining forces beats piling on driving forces.

questions.q: The strongest single restraining force is often …
questions.why: ‘Why fix what isn’t broken?’ is loudest in winning organisations.

questions.q: In Kotter’s model, steps 1–4 correspond to which Lewin phase?
questions.why: Steps 1–4 unfreeze, 5–7 move, 8 refreezes.

questions.q: Kotter’s step 1 is …
questions.why: Make ‘why now’ vivid enough that standing still feels riskier.

questions.q: ‘Declaring victory too soon’ violates which Kotter step?
questions.why: Step 7 warns the old culture flows back if you stop early.

questions.q: The key insight about Kotter is that …
options: More than half happens before anything visibly changes
questions.why: Most failed change skipped the unfreezing steps 1–4.

questions.q: Satya Nadella’s Microsoft turnaround is used to illustrate …
questions.why: Honest urgency, rebuilt coalition, clear vision, publicised wins, anchored growth mindset.

questions.q: The five steps of action research are diagnosis, analysis, feedback, action and …
questions.why: It runs change like the scientific method and ends by measuring against baseline data.

questions.q: Action research lowers resistance mainly because …
questions.why: It is problem-focused and participative, so buy-in builds before change starts.

questions.q: Two groups each writing how they see themselves and the other is which OD tool?
questions.why: Intergroup development surfaces that most of the conflict is stereotype.

questions.q: Appreciative inquiry differs from other OD tools because it starts from …
options: When we were at our best
questions.why: Its 4-D cycle (Discovery, Dreaming, Design, Destiny) builds on strengths.

questions.q: Process consultation’s distinctive value is that …
options: The manager learns to diagnose their own issues
The consultant solves it for you
questions.why: The diagnostic skill stays with the manager after the consultant leaves.

questions.q: ‘Managing paradox’ in change-ready firms means …
options: Holding tensions that never fully resolve (like a moving bicycle)
questions.why: Balance exists only with forward momentum; tensions are held, not solved.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four conditions that stimulate innovation?
questions.why: The four are organic structures, innovation rewards, slack resources and cross-boundary communication.

questions.q: An ‘idea champion’ is someone who …
options: Actively fights an innovation through resistance
questions.why: Champions provide the energy and political push to get ideas adopted.

questions.q: A learning organisation is characterised by …
options: Continuous capacity to adapt; systems thinking and shared vision
questions.why: It discards old routines, thinks in systems and subordinates personal agendas.

questions.q: Stress is defined as a condition where an outcome is both …
questions.why: Stress lives in the gap between demands and resources when stakes are high.

questions.q: High demands with high resources are experienced as …; high demands with low resources as drowning.
questions.why: Resources convert a heavy load into an energising challenge.

questions.q: That a trivial last request can trigger a huge reaction shows stressors are …
questions.why: Each stressor adds to the pile; the small one is just the last straw.

questions.q: Red tape, office politics and unclear responsibilities are …
questions.why: Hindrance stressors block goals and only corrode; challenge stressors can energise.

questions.q: A leader’s job regarding stress is best described as …
options: Strip out hindrance stress so challenge remains
questions.why: Keep the energising challenge, kill the corrosive hindrance.

questions.q: Which stress symptoms form a leader’s most usable ‘dashboard’?
questions.why: You can’t see blood pressure, but you can see absences and output.

questions.q: The cumulative ‘wear and tear’ from constant adjustment is …
questions.why: Allostasis is the adjusting; allostatic load is the accumulated cost.

questions.q: The inverted-U stress model should be used cautiously because it is …
questions.why: Intuitive but not well backed by evidence.

questions.q: The best-documented buffer against stress is …
questions.why: Collegial and social support is the most reliable moderator of stress.

questions.q: Even high earners reporting money troubles reflects that overextension …
questions.why: Lifestyle and commitments often rise with earnings; it’s a personal-life stressor.

questions.q: The cheapest organisational stressor for a leader to fix is usually …
questions.why: Clarifying who owns what costs little and is largely within the leader’s signature.

questions.q: The single thing Jess Westerly must NOT do next is …
questions.why: Repeating the original mistake — or leading with cash — would deepen the failure.

questions.q: Kauflauf’s field consultants are notable because they rank money … among motivators.
questions.why: This sales force runs on pride and storytelling, so cash is the wrong first lever.

questions.q: Jess’s analysis (35% of time on 85%-revenue clients) being excellent yet failing shows …
options: Being right wins approval up, but relationships/systems win adoption down
questions.why: Correct diagnosis is the entry ticket, not the victory.

questions.q: ‘Karoshi’, the anchor story of the stress section, refers to …
questions.why: Naoya Nishigaki’s death from overwork frames stress as a leadership responsibility.

questions.q: One study found that being treated unfairly measurably raised employees’ …
questions.why: Unfair treatment is a physiological event, not just bad manners.

questions.q: The most underrated organisational stressor, per the notes, is …
questions.why: Role conflict, overload and especially ambiguity are highlighted as underrated.

questions.q: On culture and stress, the study cited found US employees stressed by lack of control while Chinese employees were stressed by …
options: Job evaluations and lack of training
questions.why: The stressors and their meaning differ across cultures.

questions.q: The professor’s three questions for any change are content, process and …
questions.why: Content = what changes; process = how; context = where. Jess ignored context.

questions.q: Jess Westerly’s core misjudgement was assuming …
options: What worked at her last company would work here (ignoring context)
questions.why: Same tool, different context, the classic expert’s error.

questions.q: Edgar Schein’s ‘process consultation’ holds that …
options: The consultant is the expert with all answers
The client system knows its work best; the consultant helps it ask the right questions
questions.why: It dissolves us-vs-them by letting the organisation diagnose itself.

questions.q: Arriving as ‘the expert’ (as Jess did) tends to …
options: Invite everyone to prove you wrong
questions.why: Expert mode fits only when the outsider truly holds knowledge insiders lack.

questions.q: Kurt Lewin developed his change model partly out of his lifelong concern with …
options: Changing attitudes toward race and prejudice (he fled Nazi Germany)
questions.why: The German-Jewish refugee studied how to shift deeply held attitudes.

questions.q: ‘Creating a burning platform’ corresponds to which Lewin stage?
questions.why: Kotter’s phrase for unfreezing; Jess skipped it entirely.

questions.q: The professor’s claim about change models is that …
options: Every model is a reworking/expansion of Lewin’s unfreeze-move-refreeze
questions.why: Branded X-Y-Z models all trace back to Lewin; Kotter’s 8 steps map onto the 3 stages.

questions.q: On who sees vs who knows the need for change: an outsider tends to …
options: See the need more readily but risk throwing the baby out with the bathwater
questions.why: Pair outsider diagnosis with insider knowledge of what actually works.

questions.q: The ‘doing well vs doing badly’ paradox of change is that …
options: A winning firm has high capability but low felt need; a losing firm the reverse
questions.why: The sweet spot is to change while still strong, which is why unfreezing winners is hard.

questions.q: In a ‘downward spiral’, each failed fix tends to …
options: Reduce decision-making ability as blame paralyses people
questions.why: Repeated failure can spin an organisation down toward dissolution (e.g. Kodak).

questions.q: The directive failing under Jess’s own name and ID meant that …
options: She, not her boss, absorbed all the blame
questions.why: The wrong messenger destroyed her credibility when it failed.

questions.q: Self-set goals generally command more commitment than assigned goals, which is why …
options: Removing the consultants’ own control over call patterns bred resistance
questions.why: Imposing a target stripped ownership the field force previously held.

questions.q: Kauflauf’s change was pushed mainly by …
options: The professional ‘grown-ups’ brought in to bring order, not a felt market need
questions.why: The firm was winning; the push came from incoming managers, so the field saw no need.

questions.q: Motivation’s three dials are intensity, persistence and …
questions.why: Intensity (how hard), direction (toward what), persistence (how long).

questions.q: Removing a hygiene problem (Herzberg) produces …
questions.why: Satisfaction and dissatisfaction are separate scales.

questions.q: In expectancy theory a zero on any link collapses motivation because the links are …
questions.why: Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence.

questions.q: Cafeteria-style rewards directly address low …
questions.why: Letting people choose the reward raises its personal value.

questions.q: Biprajeet earning more but feeling less satisfied is explained by …
options: A higher-paid referent in equity theory
questions.why: Fairness is a ratio against a referent, not an absolute number.

questions.q: In the MPS formula, the two multiplier dimensions are …
questions.why: Zero autonomy or zero feedback zeroes motivating potential.

questions.q: The Wells Fargo scandal shows goals …
options: Have a dark side when unrealistic and reward-linked
questions.why: Aggressive reward-linked goals invited mass cheating.

questions.q: The fundraiser-meets-student study illustrates …
questions.why: Seeing the beneficiary raised persistence and funds raised.

questions.q: Marcia losing her joy once paid for shelter work illustrates …
questions.why: Extrinsic reward can crowd out intrinsic interest.

questions.q: ERG’s frustration-regression explains offshore pay premiums because …
options: Frustrated relatedness regresses to existence demands
questions.why: Blocked relatedness becomes ‘then pay me more.’

questions.q: Job enrichment is rooted in which theory?
questions.why: Enrichment adds motivators — responsibility, growth, achievement.

questions.q: Asch’s experiments demonstrated …
questions.why: ~75% matched an obviously wrong group answer at least once.

questions.q: Social loafing in collectivist cultures is … than in the West.
questions.why: Collectivist members feel more responsible to the group.

questions.q: The defining difference between a work group and a team is …
questions.why: Teams produce more than the sum of inputs; groups don’t.

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of employees actually prefer teamwork?
questions.why: Teams are admired in the abstract, avoided in practice.

questions.q: The Big Five trait most important for teams is …
questions.why: Conscientious members follow through and back up teammates.

questions.q: How rule-bound a job is reflects …
questions.why: Formalisation = standardisation through written rules.

questions.q: Acme is mechanistic; Omega is …
questions.why: Fluid roles, no memos, collective decisions.

questions.q: Cutting payroll without redesigning the work produces …
questions.why: Remaining staff overloaded, morale down, knowledge lost.

questions.q: Jones’s Stage 4 dilemma is balancing standardisation against …
questions.why: Formalisation’s benefits vs the culture that built loyalty.

questions.q: ‘Profitable in what environment?’ warns that Acme’s edge depends on a … market.
questions.why: Mechanistic wins when the environment is stable.

questions.q: Boundary spanning increases …
questions.why: Communicating across group lines spreads knowledge.

questions.q: High need-for-autonomy employees thrive in … structures.
questions.why: They prefer discretion; need-for-clarity people prefer mechanistic.

questions.q: Amul is structurally …
questions.why: Local cooperatives decide locally; the federation coordinates.

questions.q: ‘Structure is strategy made visible’ means design choices …
options: Determine what the org can do and who wants to work there
questions.why: Reporting lines and rules are consequential leadership choices.

questions.q: Change management is really about managing …
options: The loss of the old (habit, status, identity)
questions.why: People mourn what change threatens, not the new tool’s merits.

questions.q: Coercion is …
options: Fast but breeds later resentment and disengagement
questions.why: Surface compliance now, underground disengagement later.

questions.q: Jess Westerly’s deepest resistance engine was …
options: Threat to power (who decides call patterns)
questions.why: Taking a decision that was theirs threatened their power.

questions.q: Being right about the data, for a change agent, is …
options: The entry ticket, not the victory
questions.why: Data wins approval up; relationships and systems win adoption down.
